item.title: Isaias Dims the Gulf Coast
item.summary: High-definition images of nighttime lights show where the hurricane knocked out power along the Florida Panhandle and how quickly the lights came back.
item.page_text:
High-definition images of nighttime lights show where the hurricane knocked out power along the Florida Panhandle and how quickly the lights came back.
After a quiet start to the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season, Isaias became the season’s first hurricane on October 8 as it tracked toward the U.S. Gulf Coast. The storm brought heavy rain and flash flooding to parts of the Southeast, including Alabama and the Florida Panhandle, and winds that toppled trees and downed power lines, leaving many people in the dark.
Isaias made landfall near Destin, Florida, on the evening of October 9 as a Category 2 hurricane with maximum sustained winds of 105 miles (170 kilometers) per hour. Gusts topped 100 miles per hour along a corridor west of the storm’s center, according to the National Weather Service, with preliminary reports showing a 117-mile-per-hour gust in Oriole Beach and a 102-mile-per-hour gust at Pensacola City Hall.
These areas of high winds overlapped a broader area west of the storm’s eye where satellite images showed substantial decreases in nighttime lights. The image pair above shows nighttime lights before and after the storm. The left image is a composite of August 2026 data representing typical conditions, and the right image shows lights on October 11, after most of the storm’s clouds had cleared.
The data depicted in the images, provided by Ranjay Shrestha of NASA's Black Marble science team , come from the Black Marble HD product. The product uses data from the VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) on the NOAA-20 satellite, which has a day-night band that detects light emitted and reflected at night. The team processed the data to account for changes in the landscape, the atmosphere, and phase of the Moon, and to filter out stray light that does not come from electric lights. Dark gray, hash-marked areas show where clouds prevented VIIRS from collecting data. The nighttime lights are shown over a base map from the Landsat 9 satellite.
“Standard Black Marble nighttime lights imagery, available through NASA Worldview , provides a broad picture of the storm's immediate impacts,” Shrestha said. “Black Marble HD takes this a step further by allowing us to visualize these changes at a much finer spatial scale.”
At these finer scales, the images reveal lights decreasing sharply around parts of Pensacola, Florida, and along the U.S. Route 98 corridor toward Destin, suggesting widespread power disruptions. Shrestha also pointed out pockets where lights persisted, including Pensacola International Airport, Pensacola Christian College, and parts of downtown Pensacola. “These patterns could reflect backup power systems, differences in electrical infrastructure, or areas that maintained electricity during the storm, although the imagery alone cannot confirm the underlying reasons,” he said.
Black Marble HD images also reveal the pace and spatial patterns of recovery. The image pair above compares the same October 11 view (left) with one from October 12 (right), when lights had begun to return to some affected areas. By October 14, lighting patterns looked similar to pre-storm conditions. “Understanding where recovery is progressing and where disruptions persist can help emergency responders and decision makers identify areas that may require additional attention, prioritize resources, and assess the effectiveness of restoration efforts,” Shrestha said. Black Marble data complement ground-based outage reports rather than replace them, offering a more comprehensive view of disasters' impacts and recovery. “Ultimately, this is where the value of Black Marble lies: turning nighttime Earth observations into actionable insights that support informed decisions and help bridge the gap between Earth science and action,” Shrestha said. The NASA Disasters Program, in coordination with FEMA and the USGS Coastal Storms Team, is supporting the Alabama Red Cross and the Alabama Emergency Management Agency’s response to Hurricane Isaias. The team will be posting maps and data products on its open-access mapping portal as new information becomes available.
NASA Earth Observatory images by Lauren Dauphin, using Black Marble HD data courtesy of Ranjay Shrestha/NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center and Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey . Story by Kathryn Hansen.

item.title: Fires Arrive in the Amazon Rainforest
item.summary: During El Niño, a cascade of fires across the tropics begins in equatorial Asia and continues in the central and eastern Amazon.
item.page_text:
During El Niño, a cascade of fires across the tropics begins in equatorial Asia and continues in the central and eastern Amazon.
Unlike a tornado or thunderstorm that can deliver destruction in minutes, El Niño exerts its influence over many months. This year, a drought accompanying El Niño has left the Amazon rainforest primed to burn, and scientists say the region has entered the early stages of what they think will be a long and severe fire season.
Starting in September 2026, satellites detected sharp increases in fire activity and smoke emissions in the central and eastern Amazon, visible in fire and emissions monitoring platforms including NASA's Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS), the Global Fire Emissions Database (GFED), and NASA Worldview . The region with elevated fire activity stretches from forests surrounding the commercial and transportation centers of Manaus and Santarém to the mouth of the Amazon River.
When the MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) on NASA's Aqua satellite captured this image of smoke streaming from fires on both sides of the Amazon River on October 12, 2026, heavy smoke socked in Manaus, the capital of the Brazilian state of Amazonas. That day, city officials reported extremely poor air quality, with fine particulate matter (PM 2.5 ) values above 135 micrograms per cubic meter, the second-worst rating on a regional air quality index . The pall disrupted daily life in a city of more than 2 million people. Schools closed, and citywide events and children's sports leagues were canceled as officials warned of hazardous air quality, according to news reports .
The burning around Santarém and Manaus is part of a "cascade" of fire in the tropics that accompanies the disrupted rainfall patterns of an El Niño , said Douglas Morton, an Earth system scientist based at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center. The pattern begins along the equator with drought and peat fires in Indonesia , followed by elevated fire activity in this part of the Amazon. Morton and colleagues from the University of California, Irvine; Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam; and the University of Maryland detailed the pattern in a 2017 study following the destructive fire season that accompanied the 2015–2016 El Niño . They also saw the pattern play out in 2023.
A swell of fire in the tropics riding the 2026 El Niño has followed the pattern. Drought, fire, and smoke have smothered parts of Indonesia since August, with hundreds of homes razed in October and thick smoke blanketing whole islands most days. "Now, in the Amazon, we're seeing the second domino in the cascade fall," Morton said, referring to the uptick in fires that has begun in Pará and Amazonas.
Morton and his colleagues expect the next wave of fire to hit farther north in November and December in the Brazilian states of Roraima, northern Pará, and Amapá, as well as parts of Venezuela, Guyana, and Suriname. Finally, around August and September 2027, he said, drought and fire risk will peak in the southern Amazon regions of Brazil and Paraguay.
"It's so striking—and frustrating—that this is happening all over again," said Morton, adding that many of the same forests that burned during the El Niño events in 2023 and 2015 are burning again. Forest fires in these rainforests are known to cause especially serious ecological damage because most species are not adapted to fire. It's likely that some of the forest fires will burn even more intensely this time because the earlier fires partially charred trees, degrading the forest and making what remained more susceptible to burning, he added.
Morton expects the fires around Santarém and Manaus to continue burning until the rainy season arrives in December 2026 or January 2027. For the regions to the north and south, there is still time to prepare. "Given the intensity of this El Niño, this really is the year for people to avoid burning at all costs," Morton said.
It's so wet in the Brazilian Amazon that lightning ignites less than 1 percent of fires, so the vast majority of fires currently burning there were started by people, Morton said. But this year's drought, worsened by El Niño, has been intense. Brazil's National Institute of Meteorology reported that Manaus rainfall levels were 95 percent less than normal in August and 60 percent less than normal in September .
The large fires in this region began as management fires—clearing shrubs from pastures or crops from fields, for instance—but have escaped and are now burning freely through the parched understory of the rainforest, he added. Analysis of satellite observations indicates there are 50 to 70 uncontrolled fires burning in the Santarém region alone, said Shane Coffield, a University of Maryland assistant research scientist at NASA Goddard.
As part of a NASA Earth Action project , Coffield is mining fire observations from VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) to identify fires that didn't meet the threshold for inclusion in official data products distributed by FIRMS. He plans to share the locations of these "candidate fires" with scientists at MapBiomas , a multi-institutional network comprising universities, NGOs, and technology companies that maps fires and land-use change in the Amazon.
"For the area around Santarém, we've identified about 40 percent more fires than you'll see in active fire counts from FIRMS," said Coffield. Satellites often miss fires in circumstances like this due to dense smoke, clouds, and tree canopy cover, which can block the sensors from detecting the infrared signal of fires—especially lower-intensity fires spreading along the forest understory. "On some of the smokiest days, we have very few detections from MODIS and VIIRS, and we know that isn't right."
NASA Earth Observatory images by Lauren Dauphin, using MODIS data from NASA EOSDIS LANCE and GIBS/Worldview . Story by Adam Voiland.

item.title: Satellite Images Show Extent of Trump Admin’s Tree-Felling at DC Golf Course
item.summary: Sign up here to receive Bellingcat’s biggest investigations by email as soon as they are published. Satellite imagery obtained by Bellingcat lays bare the extent of tree-felling at a Washington DC golf course that President Trump is reportedly seeking to transform into a championship-level course, despite moves to protect the site by conservationists. The extent […]
item.page_text:
Jake Godin is a researcher for Bellingcat. He has covered multiple conflicts with an emphasis on geolocation, munition identification and documenting civilian harm. Prior to joining Bellingcat, he worked at Scripps News on open source reporting, some in partnership with Bellingcat.
Eoghan Macguire is lead editor at Bellingcat. He previously worked at CNN, NBC News and Storyful. Twitter: @eoghanmacguire.
Sign up here to receive Bellingcat’s biggest investigations by email as soon as they are published .
Satellite imagery obtained by Bellingcat lays bare the extent of tree-felling at a Washington DC golf course that President Trump is reportedly seeking to transform into a championship-level course, despite moves to protect the site by conservationists.
The extent and circumstances surrounding the rapid changes prompted a judge to call an emergency hearing earlier this week, banning any further changes until later this month.
Reports on Wednesday detailed that 430 trees were cut down at the East Potomac Golf Links  which is owned by the Federal government and managed by the National Park Service (NPS) . This is despite a judge reportedly stating earlier this year that no more than 10 trees at the course could be cut down without first notifying the court.
NPR reported that officials notified the court just before 5pm on Friday Oct. 9 of plans to remove up to 529 trees in phases starting  the next day on Saturday Oct. 10. That prompted US District Court Judge Ana Reyes to call an emergency hearing on Oct. 12. By that time, 430 trees had reportedly been cut down.
Reyes is reported to have said she was “ furious ” with the Justice Department for the lack of time afforded the court and plaintiffs before the tree removal was carried out.
She was also reported to have said that the government’s actions had cost it “all of its credibility with me in this case.”
Images taken at the course earlier this week show trunks and branches strewn out across fairways.
Just total devastation wrought on East Potomac Park this past weekend. 

450+ trees. For an admin that professes to support “beautification” of DC, that’s sure not what we or anybody else who has seen what they did on Saturday would describe it as. 

East Potomac is (was?) a thriving, beautiful gem in the heart of Washington DC. A beautiful, public, accessible place that hundreds of thousands use annually. The assault on this place should infuriate every American. 

The impacts of what took place Saturday will take years to fix. We cannot sit idly by while this admin treats our public lands like they are for the taking.
But satellite imagery affords a broader look at exactly what sections of the course have been impacted.
The Image below from Planet Labs taken on October 8 shows the golf course before the tree-felling was carried out.
Planet Labs imagery captured on Oct. 13 shows large barren sections towards the south and west of the course, where trees were removed.
A before and after slider allows for easy comparison of the Oct. 8 and Oct.13 images.
Your donations directly contribute to our ability to publish groundbreaking investigations and uncover wrongdoing around the world.
Reuters reported that an organisation called The ​DC Preservation League said in a February ​2026 lawsuit that President Donald Trump was flouting ⁠environmental laws to “irreparably destroy a priceless piece of American history” so he could “convert a public recreation space into an exclusive, high-end golf course.”
Kevin Griess, an NPS official, reportedly stated at Monday’s hearing that tree removal was part of a 2019 plan that predates Trump’s aims for the course and sought to restore links-style vegetation.
Bellingcat contacted NPS as well as the Department of Justice but did not receive a response before publication.
The changes to the golf course are not the only ones President Trump has sought in Washington DC and the surrounding area since the beginning of his second term. In October last year  demolition began on the East Wing of the White House with the aim of building a new ballroom claiming it was “the safest building ever built.”
Trump has also proposed a 250-foot-tall “ Triumphal Arch ” to be built just outside the Arlington National Cemetery in Virginia.
Correction: This article was updated on October 15 to reflect that a judge told the US government not to cut down more than 10 trees before providing notice. The article previously said that no more than 10 trees could be felled without the court’s approval. The headline has also been changed to reflect this.

item.title: Hurricane Simon Lurks Off the Mexican Coast
item.summary: Though it remained offshore, the storm lashed coastal areas with high winds and flooding—and produced remarkable rippling patterns in the upper atmosphere.
item.page_text:
Though it remained offshore, the storm lashed coastal areas with high winds and flooding—and produced remarkable rippling patterns in the upper atmosphere.
Hurricane Simon, the latest in a long progression of tropical cyclones in the Eastern Pacific this season, passed close to the Mexican coast as a category 4 storm on October 11, 2026. Sustained winds reached 250 kilometers (155 miles) per hour as it crept north-northwest.
Simon’s eye was about 50 kilometers (30 miles) offshore, between Manzanillo and Puerto Vallarta, when the VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) on the Suomi NPP satellite acquired this image around 2:30 p.m. local time (20:30 Universal Time) on October 11.
By that time, sustained winds were about 210 kilometers (130 miles) per hour, according to the National Hurricane Center (NHC), and the storm’s inner core was brushing up against the coast. The topography of the Sierra Madre mountains appeared to temper the storm’s intensity somewhat and shrink the size of its wind field, the NHC noted. Still, the major hurricane delivered heavy rain and flooding to coastal areas, including the port city of Manzanillo, and raised the risk of mudslides in mountainous areas, according to news reports .
In the early morning hours of October 11, satellites captured the storm’s effects extending into the upper atmosphere . This nighttime image (above), acquired with VIIRS on the NOAA-21 satellite, shows atmospheric gravity waves radiating from the hurricane. These ripples form when latent heat released near the tropical cyclone’s eyewall drives strong convection, building tall cumulonimbus clouds with updrafts that can send waves into the stratosphere and mesosphere.
But these waves are not always observable. Winds in the upper atmosphere can dissipate them before they reach the mesosphere, where they show up as ripples in airglow—faint light emitted by gases at those high altitudes. The VIIRS day-night band is sensitive to airglow but also detects reflected moonlight, which can wash it out. On the night this image was acquired, minimal illumination from the Moon helped the airglow stand out.
On the morning of October 13, forecasts of Simon’s intensity and path remained “very low confidence,” as the storm’s evolution continued to defy meteorologists’ expectations . The system may steer north and enter the Gulf of California before making landfall. Large swells causing dangerous nearshore conditions were expected along portions of the southwestern and west-central coasts of Mexico in the coming days.
NASA Earth Observatory images by Michala Garrison, using VIIRS data from NASA EOSDIS LANCE , GIBS/Worldview , the Suomi National Polar-orbiting Partnership , and the Joint Polar Satellite System (JPSS). Story by Lindsey Doermann.

item.title: An Impact Structure With Legs
item.summary: If the thought of extraterrestrial objects crashing into Earth weren’t creepy enough, behold Australia’s Spider Crater.
item.page_text:
If the thought of extraterrestrial objects crashing into Earth weren’t creepy enough, behold Australia’s Spider Crater.
Editor's Note: Today's story is the answer to the October Puzzler .
From above, the mere appearance of a curious geologic feature in Western Australia is enough to cause a fright. The aptly named Spider Crater, the product of a meteorite impact followed by hundreds of millions of years of erosion, sprawls across the landscape in the country’s Kimberley region .
The OLI (Operational Land Imager) on the NASA-USGS Landsat 9 satellite captured this image of the crater on September 20, 2026. The full impact structure has an oval shape measuring about 13 kilometers by 11 kilometers (8 miles by 7 miles), with the spiderlike central portion measuring about 4 kilometers (2.5 miles) across.
Geologists believe the unusual arachnoid pattern is the remnant of a central uplift , the raised portion of the crater floor that formed in the rebound of the initial impact shock. The light-colored “legs” are sandstone ridges that have endured while other rock layers in the impact zone have eroded away.
For decades after the feature’s discovery, scientists struggled to weave a tale about its formation. Some proposed it had a volcanic past. But with some legwork in the field, geologists identified telltale signs of a past impact: fan-shaped fractures called shatter cones . These fractures form only when intense shock waves travel through rock, and they are ubiquitous in Spider Crater’s central dome.
Scientists have subsequently performed lab analyses of shocked quartz and zircon crystals from the sandstone, which can help them reconstruct the angle of the meteorite’s impact. The date of the impact is uncertain, but estimates based on rocks in the region place it between about 900 million and 600 million years ago—making Spider Crater a creature of the late Precambrian.

Of all the questions we ask of a map, perhaps none is more fundamental than this one: Where are the people?
It sounds like a question we should have answered long ago. Yet in an age of seemingly ubiquitous, real-time information, our picture of where humanity actually lives remains surprisingly blurry. Censuses are expensive, infrequent and, in many places, badly out of date. Cities across the Global South are growing far faster than their residents can be counted. Conflict, disaster, and climate stress are setting millions of people in motion. The result is that many of the world's most vulnerable communities are, in effect, invisible – and on a volatile, warming planet, invisibility can be fatal.
In early 2024, we announced a collaboration with the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME) at the University of Washington and Microsoft's AI for Good Lab to help close that gap. Today, I'm delighted to share that the results of this multi-year initiative are being made widely available.
The result is Populace : a continuously updated map of the world's population, realized in unprecedented detail. Populace measures the density of human populations across the entire globe at a gridded resolution of 40 meters, updated quarterly. It is the most up-to-date, highest resolution, and most accurate population data available anywhere – and it's available now .
The population growth of Lusaka, Zambia, from 2020 to 2026, as revealed by Populace.
Populace is the product of a unique collaboration, one in which each partner Populace is the product of a unique collaboration, one in which each partner brings something singular.
It begins in orbit. Planet's fleet of satellites images the Earth's entire land mass nearly every day, providing a comprehensive, continuously refreshed record of the built environment – every new rooftop, road and settlement, wherever it appears. From that archive, we assemble high-quality, cloud-free quarterly basemaps of the planet.
Microsoft's AI for Good Lab then runs world-class machine learning models over those basemaps – trillions of pixels for every year of data – to detect where human structures are, and how their density changes over time.
Finally, IHME brings its deep expertise in spatial demography. Its researchers combine that building-density signal with census, survey, and administrative data, along with dozens of other predictors, to model how many people live in and around those structures. The result is a population estimate that remains reliable even where traditional data is sparse, stale, or missing altogether.
“At the AI for Good Lab, we believe that data and AI are among the most powerful tools we have to address the world's most critical humanitarian challenges,” said Juan Lavista Ferres, Chief Data Scientist at Microsoft and head of the AI for Good Lab. “But that potential is only realized when the right partners come together around a real problem. With Populace, we've helped turn a planet's worth of imagery into something deeply human: an understanding of where people are, so that governments and humanitarian organizations can reach them when it matters most.”
High-resolution population data is one of those rare assets whose value compounds with every new question asked of it. Some of the most important applications include:
Understanding the Geography of Public Health Risk Diseases move through populations differently depending on how those populations are clustered. Knowing precisely where people live – and how densely – helps public health officials target vaccination campaigns, site clinics, model the spread of infectious disease, and understand who is exposed to hazards like extreme heat and air pollution.
